rio_sio.title: Rio sio — Automated Robotic Inspection of Imperfections on Optical Surfaces
rio_sio.meta: Technologie Campus Teisnach Optik, TH Deggendorf · Master's Research Project
rio_sio.p1: At Technologie Campus Teisnach Optik (TH Deggendorf), I contributed to the development of a collaborative robotic inspection system for detecting microscopic imperfections on optical surfaces.
rio_sio.p2: My work combined CAD development, mechanical and optomechanical integration, optical alignment, illumination experiments, robotic positioning, manual calibration, and experimental validation.
rio_sio.p3: The system integrated a FANUC CR-7iA/L cobot, high-resolution imaging, optical metrology, and controlled illumination. Experimental results demonstrated the detection of surface defects down to approximately 6 µm.

points.title: High-Pressure Test Bench Operation
points.text: I supported the day-to-day operation of specialized high-pressure test bench systems used for industrial component evaluation. This involved conducting rigorous pre-test checks, verifying pneumatic line integrity, and ensuring all physical safety barriers were secured before pressure ramp-up.

points.title: Control of High-Pressure Oxygen and Nitrogen
points.text: Test procedures required precise regulation of high-pressure gaseous oxygen (O2) and nitrogen (N2) flows. I managed pressurized gas delivery according to standardized test protocols, maintaining stable supply pressures while monitoring pressure differentials across test specimens.

points.title: Process Monitoring via Siemens PCS 7
points.text: Real-time process surveillance was conducted using the Siemens PCS 7 industrial control system interface. I monitored continuous sensor telemetry, verified live pressure and temperature readings against allowable thresholds, and flagged any transient anomalies immediately.

points.title: Multi-Valve Sequencing and Workflow Operation
points.text: Executing the experimental test cycle involved operating an intricate sequence of manual, pneumatic, and safety relief valves. Correct valve timing was critical to prevent pressure surges, ensure smooth gas venting, and protect sensitive downstream instrumentation.

points.title: Test Monitoring and Measurement Documentation
points.text: Throughout every test run, I recorded critical sensor metrics, flow parameters, and operational runtimes into standardized engineering logs. These structured measurement logs provided an auditable data trail for subsequent engineering evaluations and quality verification.

points.title: Authoring Bilingual Operating Manuals (English & German)
points.text: A central contribution of my role was authoring comprehensive, user-friendly operating manuals in both English and German for the test bench setup. These manuals documented step-by-step operating workflows, valve sequence checklists, troubleshooting procedures, and safety guidelines for future engineers and student researchers.

points.title: Experimental Procedures & Industrial Laboratory Safety
points.text: Working with high-pressure and reactive gas systems reinforced the highest standards of industrial laboratory safety and contamination prevention. I ensured that clean gas handling protocols were meticulously followed and that all emergency isolation mechanisms remained verified and operational.

chapters.title: Understanding How Things Work
paragraphs: My fascination with engineering began long before I knew what an engineer actually did.

As a child, I loved playing with toy cars, especially those with motors, lights, and simple electronic controls. I still remember having a car that responded to clapping: one clap made it move forward, and another made it reverse.
But something interested me more than simply playing with these toys: understanding how they worked.

Usually, within a week or two of getting a new toy, I would find myself taking it apart. I wanted to see the motors, understand how the batteries were connected, and discover what made everything move. Sometimes I managed to put things back together. Sometimes the experiments were a little more adventurous!

One of my earliest projects was a small remote-controlled robot that I built with my cousin. It had a simple mechanism for grabbing empty bottles. Looking back, it was a modest project, but for us, making something that could actually move and interact with objects was incredibly exciting.

My curiosity wasn't limited to toys. I also loved visiting the car workshop of one of my father's friends. I would watch him repair vehicles and ask endless questions about engines, mechanical components, and how different systems worked together. He patiently explained things in a way a curious child could understand.
Those experiences stayed with me.

chapters.title: From Curiosity to Mechanical Engineering
paragraphs: When the time came to choose my university studies, the decision was surprisingly simple. I didn't seriously consider other engineering disciplines. I wanted to become a mechanical engineer.
I pursued my bachelor's degree in Mechanical Engineering in India, where I developed a stronger understanding of mechanical systems, design, manufacturing, and engineering fundamentals.
After graduating, I decided to continue my education in Germany, a country whose engineering tradition, manufacturing expertise, and technological innovation had long impressed me.
I knew that learning German would be important, so I began studying the language while I was still in India and earned my Goethe-Zertifikat B2 before moving.
In December 2020, I arrived in Germany to begin the next chapter of my journey.

Initially, I enrolled in a German-taught master's programme in Mechanical Engineering. After approximately one year, I decided to broaden my technical perspective and switched to Mechatronics and Cyber-Physical Systems at Technische Hochschule Deggendorf.
It turned out to be a meaningful decision. Mechatronics brought together several fields that had fascinated me since childhood: mechanical design, electronics, automation, and intelligent systems.

chapters.title: Engineering Beyond the Classroom
paragraphs: During my studies, I gained practical industrial experience at MAN Energy Solutions (now Everllence), and later became involved in research at Technologie Campus Teisnach Optik.
For my master's thesis, I worked on Rio sio — Automated Robotic Inspection of Imperfections on Optical Surfaces.

The project combined a FANUC collaborative robot, high-resolution imaging, optical measurement techniques, and mechanical design. It gave me the opportunity to work with real laboratory equipment, develop and integrate mechanical components, and investigate practical engineering challenges.
It was particularly rewarding because it connected theoretical engineering knowledge with physical systems that I could build, adjust, test, and improve.

chapters.title: Still Curious. Still Building.
paragraphs: My curiosity doesn't stop when the working day ends.
In my spare time, I enjoy experimenting with 3D printing, mechanical design, microcontrollers, electronics, Linux servers, and automation.

Whether I'm developing my Plottu pen plotter, designing a custom HDD enclosure, configuring a home server, or experimenting with an ESP32, I enjoy the process of taking an idea and gradually turning it into something functional.
I've also continued developing my CAD skills through additional professional training.

Today, with a master's degree in Mechatronics and Cyber-Physical Systems, research experience, and a growing collection of independent technical projects, I'm looking for an opportunity to contribute to meaningful engineering work while continuing to learn and develop.
The tools and projects have changed over the years, but the curiosity that started with those little toy cars is still exactly the same.

website_section.title: About This Website
website_section.text: This portfolio website is itself an independent engineering project. Rather than using generic templates or heavy commercial frameworks, it was designed and built as a clean, deterministic static-site architecture using standard HTML5, modern CSS with CSS custom properties, vanilla JavaScript, and a lightweight Python 3 build engine. It features native bilingual routing (EN/DE), instant switchable Light and Dark themes with zero flash, deep-link persistence, and free static hosting on GitHub Pages. AI-assisted development tools were purposefully directed to streamline build scripting, template compilation, and structured content management — demonstrating disciplined technical direction and practical problem-solving.

meta.title:
Rio sio.
Automated Robotic Inspection of Imperfections on Optical Surfaces.
meta.lead: Research project at Technologie Campus Teisnach Optik (TH Deggendorf): combining precision mechanics, collaborative robotics, calibrated imaging, and controlled multi-angle illumination.
meta.hero_caption: Kunal working with the FANUC CR-7iA/L collaborative robot during the research project.

demo.title: Rio sio in motion.
demo.intro: Demonstration of the robotic inspection workflow, including specimen positioning and optical image acquisition.

challenge.title: From human judgement to repeatable inspection.
challenge.lead: Optical surfaces are traditionally examined under controlled illumination using magnification. Distinguishing a permanent scratch or dig from removable contamination, however, is difficult, time-consuming and partly dependent on the inspector's experience.
challenge.caption_2hi: Manual visual inspection: examining an optical component under directional illumination with a magnifier.
challenge.story_p1: Could we reproduce the flexibility of a human inspector, but make positioning and image capture more consistent? The project developed an experimental robotic inspection system intended to distinguish defects from contamination on precision optical surfaces.
challenge.story_p2: The FANUC robot serves as the handling system, while a high-resolution camera, calibrated optical path, and controllable illumination reveal details that are difficult to evaluate by eye alone.

design.title: Replacing the hand, eye and light source.
design.lead: I helped design and integrate the physical inspection architecture: robot-assisted specimen handling, a high-resolution imaging assembly, an eight-direction lighting arrangement, and the mechanical structures holding these systems together.
design.caption_concept: System concept: translating manual inspection movements, magnifying optics, and directional light into robotic positioning, calibrated imaging, and controlled illumination.
design.caption_sundial: Sundial-inspired optical method for aligning the illumination angle using a shadow of defined geometry.

optics.title: When fractions of a millimetre matter.
optics.lead: To achieve useful image magnification, two objectives had to be positioned and aligned along a common optical axis. I built and adjusted experimental arrangements on a precision rail system, investigated working distances, and used interferometric measurements with a plane mirror to guide alignment.
optics.caption_6poc: Initial proof-of-concept camera and two-objective setup on an OWIS optical rail; labelled experimental arrangement.
optics.caption_6full: Close-up of the optical lens mounting and alignment arrangement after mechanical changes.
optics.caption_lab: Laboratory photograph of the optical alignment experiment on the granite surface.
optics.caption_mirror: Interferometry software capture and wavefront profile used during focal-plane and mirror alignment.
optics.note: Dual-objective optical setup aligned on an OWIS precision rail system with interferometric wavefront verification.

illumination.title: Different light directions. Different information.
illumination.lead: Light incident from different sides changes the shadows and scattering around an imperfection. I developed and calibrated the illumination arrangement so each direction could be tested individually, helping reveal how defects and particles respond under changing lighting geometry.
illumination.caption_dig: A dig illuminated from eight directions. Red arrows identify the incoming light direction for each recorded view.
illumination.caption_gp: A glass particle viewed under eight illumination directions, demonstrating direction-dependent scattering and highlights.
illumination.caption_scratch: A surface scratch / defect example under several illumination directions; compare the apparent features and shadows.
illumination.callout_p: The same feature can look very different as the illumination direction changes. This was central to experimenting with contrast, shadow geometry, and differentiation of real surface damage from surface contamination.
illumination.callout_note: Recorded experimental micrographs showing optical contrast under varying illumination angles; automated classification algorithms were developed by project partners.

mechanical.title: Designing around precision and stray light.
mechanical.lead: Beyond the optical principles, the system needed rigid mounts, accessible components, controlled wiring, and an enclosure to keep unwanted ambient light out of the inspection area. My work included CAD design, mechanical fixtures, optomechanical assembly and system integration.
mechanical.caption_cad: CAD concept for the light-shielding enclosure and structural frame.
mechanical.caption_enclosure: Actual enclosure with the FANUC inspection setup; photo taken while operating the robot at the enclosure opening.
mechanical.caption_cabinet: Project electrical cabinet illustrating the connected illumination, trigger and I/O subsystems.
mechanical.callout_p: Mechanical and optical subsystems had to be assembled, aligned, tested and revised together. Iterative CAD work and practical laboratory adjustments were an essential part of making the complete inspection arrangement usable.
mechanical.callout_note: Electrical enclosure construction and software integration were conducted in collaboration with the laboratory engineering team.

robot.title: Before automated movement came manual understanding.
robot.lead: Manual positioning and movement exploration using the FANUC teach pendant during preparation of the inspection sequence.
robot.after_video: Manual teach-pendant guidance was used to evaluate reachable coordinate envelopes around the imaging station and establish reliable motion trajectories prior to automated inspection.
robot.caption_teach: Laboratory photograph of manual robot calibration using the FANUC teach pendant.

results.title: From calibrated hardware to captured evidence.
results.lead: The integrated prototype moves an optical specimen through the inspection arrangement and records images under controlled conditions. Testing included optical alignment, inspection demonstrations and resolving-power verification with USAF 1951 targets.
results.story_p1: The Rio sio experimental system brought together collaborative robot positioning, a custom illumination architecture and high-resolution imaging in a working research demonstrator.
results.story_p2: Tests documented micron-scale inspection capability. The full thesis contains the detailed USAF target measurements, calibration procedures, experimental images and limitations.

contribution.title: What I designed, built and tested.
contribution.lead: The Rio sio initiative was conducted as an interdisciplinary R&D project at TC Teisnach Optik. This section clearly delineates my specific engineering responsibilities across mechanical design, optomechanics, and robotic commissioning.
work_items: Mechanical concept and CAD development of fixtures, mounts and the experimental structure.
Optomechanical assembly and alignment of the imaging components.
Design, integration and adjustment of multi-angle illumination hardware.
FANUC handling, manual calibration and practical robot motion/path exploration.
Experimental setup, laboratory tests, documentation and hardware troubleshooting.
contribution.collab_p1: Python image-processing software for defect identification, dimensional analysis and image stitching was developed by another student. I contributed to the physical system and experimental workflow in which those methods were used.
contribution.collab_p2: Specialized machining, cabinet wiring and other institutional support were also collaborative activities.
